summaries.example: Imagine a teacher who can see and help students in every classroom at once. That picture is not exactly what philosophers mean, because a teacher has a body and can only be in some places. The puzzle is how God could be everywhere while not being a physical body.
summaries.summary: Omnipresence is the traditional idea that God is everywhere. The entry explains why this idea is difficult: classical theism also describes God as immaterial, meaning not a physical body. A rock is in one place because its parts fill space. Philosophers such as Augustine and Anselm argued that God is not spread through space in that way. They suggested that God can be wholly present wherever God is, without being trapped or divided by a place. Aquinas explained presence using three ideas: God has power over things, knows everything, and gives things their existence. Later thinkers offered different proposals. Some compared God’s relation to the universe with a mind’s relation to its body. Others argued that God is literally located throughout space in a special way. Some added that personal presence involves shared attention or special action. The entry also points toward future study of views from many philosophical and religious traditions.
key_ideas: Omnipresence says that there is no place where God is absent.
Philosophers ask how something without a body can be present in places.
Some accounts explain divine presence through God’s power, knowledge, and role as the cause of things.
Other accounts compare the whole world to God’s body or say that God is located everywhere in a special, literal way.
A major question is whether being everywhere means being spread out in parts, as physical objects are.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic shows how one simple-sounding belief can lead to deep questions about space, bodies, knowledge, power, and existence. It also teaches us that philosophers may agree on a word while disagreeing about what the word means. Studying these different explanations helps us compare ideas carefully without pretending that one answer has been settled.

important_terms.definition: The idea that God is present everywhere.
Not made of physical matter and not having a body like an animal or person.
Having power over something, such as being able to make or change what happens.
Knowing what is happening.
The reason something exists or continues to exist.

questions_to_think_about: Can something be present somewhere without taking up space like a chair does?
Would knowing everything in a room be the same as being in the room?
If God is everywhere, would God be in empty space too?
Why might someone compare the world to a body?
Which explanation seems clearest to you, and why?

summaries.example: Suppose a person controls every movement of a robot and receives immediate information about everything the robot detects. One might use this as an analogy for divine presence, but it is incomplete: the person still acts through a physical device, while traditional accounts describe God as immaterial. The comparison raises the central issue of whether knowledge and causal power are enough for literal presence.
summaries.summary: The entry examines divine omnipresence as the claim that God is present everywhere, while noting that this claim has several possible interpretations. The main difficulty arises within classical theism: God is said to be immaterial, yet presence is ordinarily understood spatially. Material objects occupy regions through their parts, are contained by those regions, and are not wholly present in every subregion. Augustine and Anselm therefore reject a bodily, spread-out model. They maintain that God can be wholly present wherever God is without being confined by place, though the positive account remains difficult to specify. Aquinas gives a more developed traditional analysis. God is present by power because creatures are subject to divine power, by knowledge because everything is immediately open to divine awareness, and by essence because God is the cause of their existence. On this approach, divine presence is related to ordinary presence by analogy. Modern proposals develop or challenge this framework. Hartshorne and Swinburne emphasize immediate knowledge and direct agency, with Hartshorne accepting the world as God’s body and Swinburne later rejecting embodiment as misleading. Critics argue that these accounts may not distinguish presence in things from control of empty regions. Alternative theories appeal to higher dimensions, the constitution of space, or a literal form of occupation in which an entity is wholly present throughout a region. Other philosophers add personal conditions such as second-person experience, shared attention, or special action. The entry concludes that future work should broaden the largely Western monotheistic focus of the literature.
key_ideas: The classical problem is to reconcile God’s omnipresence with divine immateriality and with the fact that physical objects occupy space through their parts.
Augustine and Anselm distinguish God’s presence from being contained or divided by a place; God can be wholly present without being circumscribed by space.
Aquinas analyzes presence through power, knowledge, and essence, where essence concerns God’s being the cause of created things. This makes “present” analogical when applied to God.
Hartshorne and an early proposal by Swinburne emphasize immediate knowledge and direct causal power, but their approaches raise questions about whether the universe is thereby God’s body.

Other proposals include treating space as constituted by divine omnipresence, placing God in a higher-dimensional relation to our space, or understanding omnipresence as a special kind of literal occupation.
Some philosophers argue that knowledge and power alone do not capture personal presence; they add ideas such as second-person awareness, shared attention, or distinctive divine action.
summaries.why_it_matters: Omnipresence connects philosophy of religion with metaphysics: the study of space, location, objects, causation, mind, and personal relations. The debate illustrates how philosophical analysis can separate several questions hidden inside one doctrine: whether God is spatially located, whether divine presence is literal or analogical, whether God is present in things or merely related to them, and whether personal presence requires interaction. It also raises a methodological issue: accounts developed within a narrow historical tradition may need comparison with a wider range of ancient, modern, Jewish, Islamic, Eastern, and global perspectives.

important_terms.definition: The divine attribute of being present at every place, though philosophers disagree about what “present” means for an immaterial being.
The view that God is not composed of matter or bodily parts.
The capacity to bring about or control effects; in some accounts, God is present where divine power extends.
Awareness of what occurs; some theories explain presence through God’s immediate knowledge of events everywhere.
The relation by which something explains why another thing exists; Aquinas connects divine presence with God causing the existence of creatures.
Using a term in a related but not identical sense in different contexts, rather than with exactly the same meaning or with unrelated meanings.
The view that God’s relation to the universe resembles a mind’s relation to its body, with the world treated as God’s body.
Hudson’s proposed way for an object to be wholly located throughout a region and each of its subregions, rather than being distributed by having parts in different places.

questions_to_think_about: Does analogical use of “present” explain omnipresence, or does it avoid the ordinary meaning of presence?
If God knows and controls an occupied region in exactly the same way as an empty region, what would make an object part of God’s body?
Can something be immaterial yet literally located throughout space? What would “located” mean in that case?
Would a theory of omnipresence be incomplete if it described knowledge and power but not personal relationship?
How might including Jewish, Islamic, Eastern, ancient, or modern philosophical traditions change the study of omnipresence?

summaries.example: Think about a school principal who can know what happens in every classroom and can send instructions to any classroom. The principal would not literally be in every room. This helps show why some philosophers distinguish ordinary location from presence through knowledge and power. But it also leaves a question: if God is present in empty places as well as occupied ones, is knowledge and power enough to explain omnipresence?
summaries.summary: Omnipresence means that God is present everywhere, but philosophers disagree about what that presence involves. The problem becomes especially sharp in classical theism, which describes God as immaterial. A physical object is located by occupying space with its parts. If God has no body, then God cannot be everywhere simply by being spread across the universe like air or water. Augustine and Anselm argue that God is not contained by places and can be wholly present without being divided. Aquinas develops a traditional explanation. God is present by power because everything is under divine power, by knowledge because everything is known directly, and by essence because God causes created things to exist. This use of “present” is often called analogical: it is connected to ordinary presence but does not mean exactly the same thing. Other philosophers offer different views. Hartshorne compares the world to God’s body because God knows and controls it immediately. Swinburne explores a related idea using direct action and direct knowledge, though he later says embodiment may be a misleading description. Critics ask whether such accounts explain presence in objects, since the same knowledge and power might extend to empty regions. Newer proposals include a special kind of literal location, a higher-dimensional relation to our space, and accounts that add personal awareness, shared attention, or special action. The entry also notes that future research could include more historical, religious, and global traditions.
key_ideas: The main puzzle is how God can be everywhere while also being immaterial.
Augustine and Anselm say God is not divided into pieces or held inside space like a physical object.
Aquinas explains presence through three ideas: God’s power over things, knowledge of things, and role as the cause of their existence.
Some later philosophers compare the universe with a body that God’s mind knows and controls, while others reject that comparison.
Alternative theories say God may be literally present throughout space, related to space through extra dimensions, or present in a special way that does not make God material.
Some philosophers think presence also involves personal relations, such as shared attention or acting specially in particular places.
summaries.why_it_matters: This question matters because it tests how carefully we use words such as “place,” “body,” “know,” and “present.” It also shows why philosophers compare several explanations instead of assuming that a familiar picture must work. Learning about the debate can help students understand both the strengths and limits of analogies, and see how ideas about God are connected to broader questions about space, minds, objects, and relationships.

important_terms.definition: The belief or claim that God is present everywhere.
Not physical and not made of a body or material parts.
The ability to make things happen or control what happens.
Awareness of events or things; some theories say God knows everything directly.
The relation of explaining why something exists; Aquinas connects God’s presence with causing creatures to exist.
Using a word in a related way that is not exactly the same as its ordinary meaning.
The idea that the universe relates to God as a body relates to a mind.
A theory that God is wholly located throughout a region and its smaller regions, rather than being spread out by separate parts.

questions_to_think_about: Is being able to control something the same as being present with it?
What could it mean for God to be wholly present in many places at once?
If God is present in empty space, does that support or challenge the power-and-knowledge account?
Does calling the world God’s body clarify omnipresence or create a new problem?
Should a theory of divine presence include personal relationship as well as location?
